w: What's tested What occlusal trauma is, and primary vs secondary: healthy support vs support already lost Pushing from one side vs back and forth (jiggling), and the hourglass it makes The signs in the mouth (fremitus and others) and on the X-ray (a wider ligament space and others); a vertical defect doesn't prove it Loose teeth: what decides how loose, what loosens them, the grades, and why some looseness is the body adapting What the animal studies found: biting trauma alone, with gingivitis, with periodontitis Bite adjustment: what it does and doesn't do, and when His bottom line This lecture is Dr. Abou-Arraj's, a periodontist, the one hour of occlusion at the start of the 11/12 class. The question: does the bite hurt the gums and bone around the teeth? He told the class not to memorize the researchers' names: "Conclusions are enough." What occlusal trauma is Occlusal trauma is damage to the tooth's attachment (the ligament and bone holding it) caused by biting forces. The force starts it; the damage is what we call occlusal trauma. Primary vs secondary Primary: too much force on a tooth with healthy support, no bone or attachment lost. Secondary: normal or too much force on a tooth that has already lost support (bone and attachment loss). Think of a fence post: buried two thirds deep, leaning on it does nothing; buried only a third deep, the same lean tips it. A tooth that has lost bone pivots lower on its root, so even normal chewing can damage it. The difference is only clinical. Under the microscope, the damage looks the same in both. Pushing one way vs back and forth A one-way (unilateral) push squeezes one side of the tooth and stretches the other, and the tooth tips or moves. That's what braces do, in a controlled way. A jiggling force pushes from one side, then the other. Both sides get squeezed and stretched, and the ligament space widens on both sides into an hourglass shape, with bone loss and a loose tooth. That's usually what happens in people. A healthy reduced periodontium is gums and bone that are stable after treatment, with bone lost but no inflammation. Horizontal bone loss runs level with the line between the teeth's necks (the CEJs); vertical bone loss angles down along the root in a V. The signs Occlusal trauma can only be proven under a microscope, which we don't do on patients. So we go by signs, and it's a diagnosis, not something you see directly. In the mouth: a tooth getting looser over time; a tooth drifting out of place; fremitus, a tooth you can feel or see move when the patient taps their teeth together (rest a finger on the gum on the cheek side; it's mostly front teeth, and such a tooth is usually Class 3 loose); bite problems such as a back tooth hitting on the non-working side or a slide of more than 1 mm from CR to CO; worn spots from grinding; broken cusps or edges; and sensitivity to cold or pain when biting. On the X-ray: a wider ligament space (normal is about 0.25 mm), a thicker or broken-up lamina dura (the white line around the root), bone loss (between roots, vertical, or all around) and sometimes root resorption. His big warning: a vertical defect does not mean occlusal trauma. When trauma does come with bone loss, the loss tends to be vertical, but not the other way around. Every one of these signs can show up without occlusal trauma. Loose teeth How loose a tooth gets depends on how much bone holds it, how wide the ligament is, and its roots (one root moves more than several). Teeth get loose from gum disease, from overload (a filling or crown left high, so that tooth hits first every time: it hurts to bite and loosens), from an infection at the root tip, and after gum surgery (loose for up to a year, then they settle). To check, rock the tooth cheek-to-tongue between two instrument handles. His grades: 0, normal (0.1-0.2 mm, nothing you can see); 1, up to 1 mm side to side; 2, more than 1 mm side to side; 3, side to side and up and down (it sinks when you press on it). Dr. Givan's L7 handout numbers the grades a little differently; on both, a tooth that moves up and down is the worst grade. Looseness is often the tissues adapting to the forces. A Class 2 tooth isn't hopeless, so don't rush to pull it. Class 3 is worse. Find out why it's loose. Loose teeth heal less well after treatment (bone or gum grafts), so bring a Class 2 tooth down to Class 1 by adjusting the bite if you can. Staying loose doesn't cause gum disease, but healing is better in teeth that aren't loose. A short history A century ago, dentists thought heavy biting caused gum disease, and they ground the cusps flat to treat it. They even blamed biting for notches and rolls in the gum edge, thinking it cut off the gum's blood supply. It doesn't: the gum's blood comes from outside the bone socket, mostly from vessels running over the bone under its lining (the supraperiosteal vessels), plus the ligament and the bone. Later, studies of human remains showed gum disease is inflammation spreading from the gumline, with no sign that the bite caused it. Two later cadaver studies disagreed. One said the bite is a co-destroyer: plaque alone causes gingivitis and level bone loss, and adding heavy biting steers the damage into the ligament and bone, making vertical defects. The other said the damage follows plaque alone ("track the plaque"), with vertical defects whether or not the bite is heavy. The animal studies In the 1970s, one group used monkeys (gum disease from silk threads tied around the teeth, a wedge between teeth switched sides every 2 days) and another used beagles (bigger defects made by surgery, and a spring device that shoved a tooth out every time the dog bit and pulled it back when it opened). What they found: Biting trauma alone: looser teeth and less dense bone, but no lost attachment and no lost bone height. Take the trauma away and things go back to normal. Trauma plus gingivitis (healthy support): looser teeth, even less dense bone, still no lost attachment. Trauma plus periodontitis: the two groups disagreed. The beagles lost more attachment and bone than the disease alone caused; the monkeys didn't. Stopping the trauma let the bone grow dense again, but it didn't reverse periodontitis that was left untreated. So in animals, biting trauma doesn't cause gum disease. But animals aren't people, and the studies were short. Studies in people Early studies only looked at charts and models, and they disagreed. In gum disease research, a bite problem means a slide of more than 1 mm from CR to CO or a non-working side contact. In one trial, 50 patients with periodontitis all got full gum treatment, and half also got their bite adjusted. Two years later, the adjusted group had gained a bit more attachment (about 0.5 mm), but their pocket depths were no different, and how loose the teeth were at the start didn't matter. Some say: adjust bite problems. Others say: not every bite problem causes trauma, so choose carefully who gets adjusted. When to adjust the bite Unless it's urgent (for example, fremitus or a badly overloaded tooth at the first visit, which he might adjust right away), first treat the inflammation: home care instructions and deep cleaning. Keep watching the teeth, and at the re-evaluation, adjust the bite if they haven't improved. The bottom line Biting trauma doesn't cause gingivitis or periodontitis, but it does affect the tissues holding the teeth. There's no good evidence in people that it speeds up gum disease. On its own it makes bone less dense, not shorter, and that reverses once the force is removed. Adjusting the bite can make teeth less loose and help bone grow back, but it won't stop plaque from destroying more. Teeth that aren't loose heal better after treatment. If you adjust the bite, do it after the infection is treated, the way antibiotics are an add-on, not the first step.
